paragraphs.heading: A break that has moved
paragraphs.text: In geology, a fault is a flat fracture or break in a body of rock, where the rock on either side has been shifted a significant distance by movements of the rock mass. The large faults in Earth's crust are the work of plate tectonic forces, and the largest of them form the boundaries between the plates. Rapid movement on active faults releases energy, and that is the cause of most earthquakes. Faults can also move slowly, by what is called aseismic creep.

paragraphs.heading: Words for the parts
paragraphs.text: The fault plane is the plane that stands for the fracture surface of a fault. The fault trace, also called the fault line, is somewhere the fault can be seen or mapped at the surface, and it is the line usually drawn on geological maps to show a fault. A fault zone is a cluster of parallel faults. The same term is also used for the band of crushed rock along a single fault.

paragraphs.heading: Locking and breaking
paragraphs.text: Rocks are rigid and there is friction between them, so the two sides of a fault cannot always slide past each other easily. Now and then all movement stops. A fault plane has patches of higher friction where it becomes locked, and these are known as asperities. While a fault is locked, stress builds up. When the stress passes the strength threshold, the fault ruptures, and part of the stored strain energy is released as seismic waves. That is an earthquake.

paragraphs.heading: Hanging wall and footwall
paragraphs.text: When a fault is not vertical, its two sides have names. The hanging wall lies above the fault plane and the footwall lies below it. The names come from mining. A miner working a flat, slab-like body of ore stood with the footwall under his feet and the hanging wall over his head.

paragraphs.heading: Normal and reverse faults
paragraphs.text: These two names matter for telling apart the kinds of dip-slip fault, which are reverse faults and normal faults. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall. In a reverse fault the hanging wall moves up. The words normal and reverse were taken from English coal mining, where normal faults are the most common kind. Telling the two apart is important for working out the stress regime of the fault movement.

paragraphs.heading: Strike-slip faults
paragraphs.text: In a strike-slip fault the fault surface is usually close to vertical, and the footwall moves sideways, to the left or to the right, with very little up-and-down motion. A strike-slip fault with left-lateral motion is also called a sinistral fault, and one with right-lateral motion a dextral fault. The direction is the way the ground would be seen to move by someone standing on the other side of the fault. When a strike-slip fault forms a plate boundary it belongs to a special class, the transform fault.

paragraphs.heading: Faults that shape the land
paragraphs.text: Normal faults can leave a pattern in the landscape. A block that has dropped down between two normal faults dipping toward each other is a graben. A block left stranded between two grabens, and so between a pair of normal faults that dip away from each other, is called a horst. A run of grabens and horsts at Earth's surface gives a characteristic landscape known as basin and range topography.
